input.question: The Hubble Deep Field shoes thousands of galaxies from soon after the Big Bang. How is it we see these galaxies in every direction of the sky if the universe has expanded so much? Shouldn't they all be centred near one place in the sky? (i.e. near the Big Bang)
input.ground_truth: The Big Bang was not an event which happened in a particular location. It happened everywhere at once, and "everywhere" was a lot closer together at the time. The expansion is that everywhere is becoming more distant from everywhere else, not that things are hurtling away from some central point.

Okay, let's imagine the universe is like a big, stretchy balloon that you can draw on.

When the universe was very, very young (like a tiny balloon), everything started from one spot—kind of like the Big Bang was a tiny dot on the balloon.

Now, if you blow up the balloon (which is like the universe getting bigger), that tiny dot spreads out. But here's the cool part: every spot on the balloon looks like it's moving away from every other spot! So if you are standing on the balloon and look around, you see lots of other spots moving away from you, but from their point of view, they also see everything moving away.

The galaxies we see in the Hubble Deep Field are like little dots on the balloon that were close to the starting point a long, long time ago. But as the balloon (universe) got bigger, those dots moved far away in all directions. That’s why we see galaxies everywhere in the sky, not just in one spot—they've all moved apart as the universe grew, but from every spot, it looks like everything is spreading out.

So even though the Big Bang started in one place, the universe got so big that the galaxies are now everywhere, like dots all over a big, blown-up balloon!
